extracted.intended_audience: Undergraduate students in Math 310 (Introduction to Mathematical Reasoning); students learning how to write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Conventions and stylistic standards for writing rigorous, readable mathematical proofs in paragraph form for an undergraduate introduction-to-proof course. Covers prose style, precision, symbol/formula usage, formatting, and exposition strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in paragraph form
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof should be written in ordinary prose: complete sentences organized into paragraphs rather than terse symbolic statements or two-column proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although you may construct the proof as terse symbolic steps, the write-up must be paragraph-style. Paragraph proofs are easier for readers to comprehend than two-column proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper English
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical writing should follow conventions of grammar, punctuation, and spelling used in other formal writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use complete sentences, a period at the end of every sentence, avoid run-on sentences, ensure subject-verb agreement and parallel structure, and use correct spelling and capitalization. Non-native speakers are advised to have a native speaker review their writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs with a clear sense of who the reader is and what they already know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For this course, write as if convincing a fellow student in the class: assume the reader has the same background material but does not know the proof of the specific theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label theorems clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Each theorem proved should be clearly labeled and stated precisely in English sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use labels such as Theorem, Proposition, Lemma, Corollary to indicate the role of the result; for typesetting use boldface/italic conventions or underline in handwritten work. Choose label to signal importance or role (e.g., lemma as helper result).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show where proofs begin and end
rubrics_metrics.description: Each proof should explicitly begin with the word 'Proof' and end with QED or a terminating symbol (e.g., a square).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistently mark the start and end of proofs so the reader can see the boundaries of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Every mathematical statement must have precise meaning: terms should be well defined, conclusions justified, and symbols either defined or appropriately quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for each sentence: 'What exactly does this mean?' and 'Why exactly is this true?'. Be explicit about whether a statement is universal, existential, or about a particular object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clearly and give exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the proof is comprehensible by giving intuitive explanations and structuring longer arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For arguments longer than a few sentences, begin with an informal description of the plan, then carry it out, then summarize what you've done. State the proof method at the start if it isn't a direct proof (e.g., 'We will prove the contrapositive' or 'We will prove this by induction on n'). Intersperse sentences explaining steps when presenting a long series of equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal vs. informal parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly separate formal (definitions and logical steps) from informal (motivation, intuition, sketches) portions of the exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it easy for the reader to tell which parts are rigorous arguments and which are heuristic or motivational remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first person singular sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'I' in mathematical writing; prefer 'we' when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard practice is to use 'we' when it can reasonably mean the writer and reader (e.g., 'We will prove the theorem by induction'). Use 'I' only when referring solely to yourself (e.g., 'I learned this technique from...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid most abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use informal mathematical abbreviations in written exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common board/note abbreviations such as 'iff', 's.t.', 'w.r.t.', and 'WLOG' should not appear in formal written work. Acceptable abbreviations include standard formal ones like 'i.e.' and 'e.g.' but use them correctly (know the difference between them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical symbols judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance use of symbolic notation and prose; symbols can clarify but excessive use makes text obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single symbols and short formulas belong inline in paragraphs; large or especially important formulas should be displayed on their own centered line. Choose symbol use to improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure formulas have grammatical function
rubrics_metrics.description: Every symbol or formula must play a definite grammatical role in a sentence, typically as a noun or as a complete clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formulas as parts of sentences (e.g., 'If x > 2, we see that x^2 + x must be greater than 6.' where 'x > 2' is a clause). Read sentences aloud to check grammatical function and natural phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate displayed formulas that end sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: If a displayed formula ends a sentence, it must be followed by a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is emphasized twice in the handout as a common slip to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relation/operator symbols only to connect symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols for relations (e.g., =, >, ∈, ⊆) or operators (+, −, ∩) should connect mathematical symbols, not words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mix words and symbols like 'x is a real number that is > 2'; instead write it in words ('If x is a real number with x > 2...') or restructure so symbols connect symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format built-up expressions appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Large or built-up expressions (summations, integrals, matrices, fractions) should be displayed or written to fit naturally on a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inline fractions should use slash notation like 'x/(y+2)'; use a horizontal bar and display mode for large fractions. Small numerical fractions like 1/2 may be included inline if typeset small enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting a sentence with a mathematical symbol is poor form because symbols cannot be capitalized to mark a sentence start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reword to begin with words (e.g., 'The function f is continuous' instead of starting with 'f is continuous').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adjacent formulas without words
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place two formulas separated only by punctuation because they may appear as one long formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpose words between formulas (e.g., instead of 'If x ≠ 0, x^2 > 0' write 'If x ≠ 0, then x^2 > 0').

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit use of logical symbols in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't replace English logical words with symbols like ∃, ∀, ∧, ∨, ¬ in ordinary mathematical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such symbols only in formal symbolic logic formulas; even then, unless the subject is logic, prefer words. The symbols ⇒ and ⇔ are acceptable only to connect symbolic formulas or letters representing statements (e.g., '(a) ⇔ (b)').
